```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
```

```{r load-packages}
library(tidyverse)
library(arules)
```

## Task 1: Compute all five rule metrics from a 10,000-policyholder table

```{r task1-data}
N <- 10000
count_D  <- 6600
count_V  <- 5700
count_DV <- 2800
```

```{r task1-support}
supp_D  <- count_D  / N   # 0.66
supp_V  <- count_V  / N   # 0.57
supp_DV <- count_DV / N   # 0.28

cat("supp({Dental})  =", supp_D,  "\n")
cat("supp({Vision})  =", supp_V,  "\n")
cat("supp({D, V})    =", supp_DV, "\n")
```

```{r task1-confidence-lift}
conf_DV <- supp_DV / supp_D   # 0.424
lift_DV <- conf_DV / supp_V   # 0.744

cat("conf(D => V) =", round(conf_DV, 3), "\n")
cat("lift(D => V) =", round(lift_DV, 3), "\n")
# Lift < 1: Dental and Vision are NEGATIVELY associated.
# A Dental holder is less likely to take Vision than a randomly chosen policyholder.
# Despite 42% confidence, the rule is not actionable as a cross-sell — it goes
# against the direction of association.
```

```{r task1-conviction-leverage}
conv_DV <- (1 - supp_V) / (1 - conf_DV)
lev_DV  <- supp_DV - supp_D * supp_V

cat("conv(D => V) =", round(conv_DV, 3), "\n")  # < 1: negative dependence
cat("lev (D => V) =", round(lev_DV,  3), "\n")  # < 0: observed < expected
```

## Task 2: Trace Apriori on the 5-transaction database

```{r task2-data}
trans_list <- list(
  T1 = c("Dental", "Vision"),
  T2 = c("Dental", "Mental", "Vision"),
  T3 = c("Vision", "Maternity"),
  T4 = c("Dental", "Mental"),
  T5 = c("Dental", "Vision", "Mental")
)
N5 <- length(trans_list)
min_supp <- 0.60

contains <- function(tl, items) {
  sum(sapply(tl, function(t) all(items %in% t)))
}
```

```{r task2-pass1}
items_1 <- c("Dental", "Vision", "Mental", "Maternity")
for (item in items_1) {
  s <- contains(trans_list, item) / N5
  cat(item, ": supp =", round(s, 2), "| frequent:", s >= min_supp, "\n")
}
# L1 = {Dental (0.80), Vision (0.80), Mental (0.60)}
# Maternity (0.20) is infrequent and dropped
```

```{r task2-pass2}
for (pair in list(c("Dental","Vision"), c("Dental","Mental"), c("Vision","Mental"))) {
  s <- contains(trans_list, pair) / N5
  cat("{", paste(pair, collapse=", "), "}: supp =", round(s, 2),
      "| frequent:", s >= min_supp, "\n")
}
# L2 = {{Dental, Vision} (0.60), {Dental, Mental} (0.60)}
# {Vision, Mental} (0.40) is infrequent.
# Therefore {Dental, Vision, Mental} is pruned in Pass 3:
# its subset {Vision, Mental} is infrequent, so by the anti-monotone property
# {Dental, Vision, Mental} cannot be frequent — no scan needed.
```

## Task 3: Run apriori() and eclat()

```{r task3-convert}
trans <- as(trans_list, "transactions")
inspect(trans)
```

```{r task3-apriori}
rules_ap <- apriori(trans, parameter = list(supp = 0.40, conf = 0.60, minlen = 2))
inspect(sort(rules_ap, by = "lift"))
```

```{r task3-eclat}
freq_sets   <- eclat(trans, parameter = list(supp = 0.40, minlen = 2))
rules_eclat <- ruleInduction(freq_sets, trans, confidence = 0.60)
inspect(sort(rules_eclat, by = "lift"))
```

## Task 4: Compare Apriori and ECLAT results

```{r task4-compare}
# Both algorithms find the same set of frequent itemsets and rules —
# the output is mathematically identical. The difference is computational:
# ECLAT uses a vertical data format (tidset: set of transaction IDs per item),
# allowing fast intersection-based support counting without repeated full scans.
# For n = 500,000 rows with many items, ECLAT is substantially faster than
# Apriori because it avoids generating and scanning large candidate sets.
# For a 5-transaction toy example the difference is immeasurable.

# Top 5 by lift from Apriori
cat("--- Apriori ---\n")
inspect(head(sort(rules_ap,    by = "lift"), 5))

cat("--- ECLAT   ---\n")
inspect(head(sort(rules_eclat, by = "lift"), 5))
```
